title: Nitto in Fukushima, Japan: Multi-Generational Mingei 民芸 – John Watson
content:
Visiting Nitto in Fukushima, Japan was a dream Shop Visit for John. After Bespoked Osaka and before the Circles Ridealive weekend, Cari and John, along with Paul from Slow Spin Society, embarked on a week-long road trip to visit Japan’s most iconic cycling manufacturers. Partnering with Sim Works, today The Radavist and Slow Spin Society are telling the tale of Nitto, with its multi-generational operations, stemming from the Japanese philosophy of Mingei…

Visiting Japanese Manufacturers

Over the next three days, we’ll be looking behind the scenes at Japanese manufacturing, focusing on three legendary component manufacturers: Nitto, MKS, and Honjo. These posts will be a collaborative effort between The Radavist and Slow Spin Society with me writing about the manufacturing process and Paul interviewing people from each company.

Going into this road trip, fresh off of my Bespoked Osaka coverage, I was already thinking of an angle for this series looking at my iPhone calendar app. We were visiting Nitto on Monday, Honjo the following day, and MKS on the third day. This has been a lifelong dream of mine but, like everything, I was nervous about both the brands’ expectations and my own.

Chatting with Sim Works brand director, Masashi Kimura, about Japanese manufacturing in a post-Bespoked conversation that lasted for hours, he said something that resonated with me. As someone who is an observer of manufacturing, there is a distinct approach present in Japan that differs from Western manufacturing, but I hadn’t put my finger on it quite yet.

Starting at Cost, Not Margin

Masashi summed it up beautifully, stating, “The uniqueness of Japanese manufacturing starts at the cost, not the margin.” He continued, “In the States and Europe, they start at the margin; say 33% for product, 33% for distributor, 33% for the shop.” The 30/30/30 split works, but it can put pressure on the manufacturer to come in at a certain number and cut corners in doing so. When you’re beholden to a 30% margin, your focus is misaligned.

“Japanese manufacturers start at cost. We add a reasonable margin to the cost total for the wholesale pricing. And we’re making more numbers in production, so it works out. Then, a dealer adds 30%, and that’s the final MSRP. In doing so, we know that a higher cost is going to equate to a better product. Toyota, another Japanese manufacturer, also does this. Products from brands like Nitto, MKS, and Honjo last for decades, just like Toyota. They live longer in the market.” Kimura-san explained.

Cost-based manufacturing allows for easy adjustment for material or labor costs, and when you’re making thousands of units, it guarantees a reasonable profit margin for the company and 30% for the dealer. Cost of steel on the rise? Just bake it into the cost. Luckily, Japanese steel production and costs have been fairly stable.

Money, however, isn’t the sole motivator for makers in Japan. Along with the concept of ikigai, 生きがい, or a “reason for being,” manufacturers are a part of a bigger picture concept known as mingei.

Mingei 民芸

In the mid-1920s, Yanagi Sōetsu conceptualized the philosophy of mingei in Japan together with ceramic artists. Mingei (民芸) roughly translates to “craft of the people” in English, and it was a conscious attempt to distinguish functional utensils from “higher” forms of fine art.

There’s a certain aspect of anonymity to the philosophy. Whereas fine art shines a light on the artist as much as the artwork, mingei focuses on the utensils’ anonymity, being crafted by a group of people. This philosophy embodies the craft of Nitto, the 103-year-old component manufacturer.

Nitto 日東 History

Founded on February 11, 1923, by Masae Yoshikawa, this historic Japanese manufacturer of high-end bicycle cockpit and utility components began in the Arakawa Ward, Tokyo, Japan. The name “Nitto” (日東) comes from “日” (sun) and “東” (east), reflecting Masae Yoshikawa’s wish for the company to always rise like the sun.

While Nitto rose in 1923, it shifted to manufacturing bicycle handlebars in 1925, and future products rolled out of the factory over the following decades. In 1973, the brand moved to a brand new factory located in Nihonmatsu, Fukushima Prefecture, where it still operates today.

Masae Yoshikawa’s grandchild, Akira Yoshikawa, currently serves as president, with Akira’s son, Takahisa Yoshikawa, acting as the managing director.

Rajio Taisō ラジオ体操

For almost 100 years, the Japanese government has run a morning radio program called Rajio Taisō every morning. Directed at the health of its citizens and workforce, most companies begin their day with the calisthenics program. Upon our arrival at the Fukushima factory, we were greeted with a display of Nitto workers stretching in unison that I’ll not soon forget.

As soon as the program ended, the workers took to their stations and began production. Akira and Takahisa introduced themselves, and we convened in a back office where one of its seatposts was undergoing ISO testing. Akira began explaining how in-house testing helps keep the brand on top of quality control, while informing future design decisions.

In-House ISO Testing

He pointed to the Nitto post, in some sort of pneumatic medieval torture device, noting that most seat posts use M6 hex screws but will almost always fail on this machine, which tests at an MTB level of certification. So they use M7 instead for more strength on their “all terrain” posts. A standard post undergoes 100,000 cycles, but Nitto runs this twice.

Outside the office, a similar device housed a 1980s steel mountain bike frame with Nitto racks. Weight is loaded in the panniers and on the rack surface itself. Running at 600 cycles per minute with a 5 kilo load, the racks jostled aboard the bike frame. This will run for 100,000 times, again, twice what the standard ISO testing requires. Nitto will run its ISO testing on handlebars often 4x the required cycles, just to see where they will break.

Remarking on how old the frame was, Akira noted: “That frame has been in the machine for 30 years.” An employee added, “We tried to use a modern frame, but it broke after a week, pointing to the split steerer tube and cracked chainstay on a frame from a popular steel bike manufacturer.” Everyone in our small group grimaced.

NJS 競輪 Manufacturer

While other bicycle component manufacturers often rely on military products to keep the lights on, Nitto is proud that it “has never made machines or tools for killing people” and instead is largely supported by its manufacturing contract of NJS-approved components for Keirin, or 競輪 racing.

Keirin is Japan’s national track bike racing circuit, supported by the Japanese government and bet on like horse racing by the Japanese people. The demands of Keirin are extreme, and manufacturing products with the coveted NJS stamp of approval requires thorough testing through the Nihon Jitensha Shinkōkai certification process.

Currently, Nitto manufactures stems, handlebars, and seatposts for Keirin, with its steel B123 handlebars owning 100% market dominance. It also does all of its own ISO testing in-house to ensure its products meet the demands of Keirin. Needless to say, NJS production keeps Nitto’s production busy.

Aging Facilities

My time at Nitto was a dream come true. As a lifelong bike geek and a fan of documenting makers, I’ve owned several of its products, so seeing where and how they were made, while being able to document them, scratched both sides of my creative brain. After a few hours of photographing the space, I couldn’t help but acknowledge something: Nitto’s facilities and its workforce had aged and were in need of rejuvenation.

The factory was built in 1973 and shows its age in what one might call, politely, a patina of oxidation. On our visit, it was raining, and various buckets were catching water as it leaked from the roof. Its steel façade was pitted and rusted, and in some areas the factory’s dark and moody demeanor wasn’t intentional; the light bulbs are too difficult to replace for the workers.

Aging Workforce

But the most apparent sign of age is the brand’s workforce, with 25% of the workforce being over 70 years of age. Nitto’s factory has 42 employees and 8 work in its Tokyo-based offices. The move to Fukushima in the early 70s was decided after a failed relocation attempt higher in the mountains outside of Tokyo due to too much snow and a desire from local farmers interested in factory work. 50 years later, hiring younger people has been very difficult.

Akira explained the difficulties Nitto faces when hiring young workers. “Young people don’t want to live in the countryside; they want to live in the city,” he noted, while pointing out that “countryside living is cheaper. You’ll have a better quality of life – you’ll be closer to nature, too.”

Currently, Nitto relies on graduates from the Tokyo College of Cycle Design, where it landed its newest framebuilder, Jamin, who is eager to modernize Nitto’s offerings. “Nitto’s biggest challenge right now is making frames,” Akira noted as we talked about manufacturing hurdles. Looking over the perfect welds, Jamin leaned in to say, “They are not perfect; these are samples.” They looked perfect to me.

Mountain Biking

When I asked Akira what his proudest moment was, he promptly replied with “Developing the Slingshot stem for mountain bikers in the US market.” The Slingshot proved to be a challenge for Nitto, who, after meeting with Tom Ritchey and Gary Fisher, knew the mountain bike market was going to explode.

“Meeting Tom Ritchey and Gary Fisher led to Nitto making MTB components, and still to this day, it was our biggest challenge at Nitto. Everything was new to us. We had to start from scratch, from the materials to the designs; we’d never done anything like this before.”

When Tom visited Nitto in the late 1980s, he taught this woman, Mrs. Noriko Yabashi, to braze. She uses half as much filler as the other brazers on staff and holds her torch the same way Tom does.

Tom Ritchey’s Bullmoose design was time-intensive, and he was always looking for ways to offload intense workflows like building Bullmoose bars. After a handlebar slipped while Tom was racing Repack in 1978, he designed the Bullmoose. And by late 1980, Nitto was already manufacturing fillet-brazed Bullmoose bars for Ritchey.

In 1983, the Nitto-designed and built Slingshot stem debuted on Specialized mountain bikes. The same year Shimano launched its Deore “Deer Head,” the brand’s first MTB groupset.

Lifelong Legacy

Spending the day with Akira and Takahisa, the father and son represent a modern trope: an experienced elder running the business while an enthusiastic younger person waits to take over the reins. Akira speaks of Nitto’s founder, his grandmother Masae Yoshikawa, with great honor, and you can feel his pride in the company.

Akira has designed, engineered, and marketed a number of legacy products during his time running the company. When I asked who designed and engineered Nitto’s new products, he replied simply, “I do it all.” At 78 years old, he’s still got a pep in his step and was constantly tapping on his watch during our tour as we pried into the various stages of manufacturing with our cameras.

Takahisa, 46, is still learning under his father, and he has big shoes to fill. He hopes to take the company into the future and cut down on backorders and long lead times. Currently, Nitto’s manufacturing is months out, and that’s Takahisa’s number one priority. On top of Nitto’s own line, they also make components for a dozen other third-party companies, including Sim Works.

Shige, in 2016, at the SimWorks offices in Nagoya

Sim Works

Tanaka-san from Circles launched Sim Works in 2009, as an attempt to inject fresh designs into Nitto’s catalog. Currently, the best-selling bar in Nitto history remains its B123 bar, the professional Keirin racing, NJS-approved handlebar. Sim Works’ first collaboration handlebar with Nitto was the John B Bar, which was the B123 shape, updated for a 31.8 clamp.

Sim Works took the legacy of Nitto’s bars and updated them with new specs, rolling out seven of its own handlebar models. Nitto also makes Sim Works stems, spacers, racks, and Sim Drops bar ends.

The Radavist x Slow Spin Society

As The Radavist celebrates its 20th anniversary of covering cycling communities, we wanted to partner with the next generation of cycling media on a lifelong dream trip of mine. We’ve featured Paul from Slow Spin Society on the website before. As a wearer of many hats – Paul also works for Sim Works as its Euro branch and was gracious enough to act as our Japanese translator during the trip – Paul is always balancing his job at Sim Works with Slow Spin. As we were chatting about what a possible collaboration would look like, we landed on the concept of storytelling and interviews.

Paul wanted to focus on interviewing people at Nitto, mostly the younger people, about how they got involved in working in manufacturing at Nitto. Fukushima, where Nitto is based, is very rural and about a three-hour drive north from Tokyo in the mountains. Being a young person usually means you want to be in a city, experiencing all the excitement of an urban environment, so what drove these young people to give up the city life for rural work in manufacturing?

Roll on over to Slow Spin Society to find out!
